# Corpus Frequency Distributions {#sec-appendix-corpus-freq}

The figure below compares the frequency distributions of the approximately 47,000 corpus binomials in the BabyLM training corpus (150M tokens, 20 epochs) and the Pile, illustrating the stark difference in lexical coverage between the two training regimes. BabyLM's distribution is dominated by singleton binomials (70.7% appear exactly once), while Pile frequencies span several orders of magnitude.

```{r}
#| label: fig-corpus-freq
#| fig-pos: "H"
#| fig-cap: "Frequency distributions for the ~47K corpus binomials in the BabyLM training corpus (150M tokens, 20 epochs) and the Pile. Left: histogram of log$_{10}$ raw counts. Right: rank-frequency plot treating counts as a probability distribution (probability = count / $\\sum$ counts); both axes log-scaled. BabyLM's distribution is heavily concentrated at a single occurrence per pair (70.7% of pairs appear exactly once), whereas Pile frequencies span several orders of magnitude with a median of 365 occurrences per pair."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.2

corpus_freq_df <- local({
  babylm_raw <- read_csv("../Data/corpus_binomials.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
    mutate(freq = freq_w1_w2 + freq_w2_w1) |>
    filter(freq > 0) |>
    select(word1, word2, freq) |>
    mutate(corpus = "BabyLM (150M tok, 20 ep)")

  pile_raw <- read_csv("../Results/corpus_binomials_infinigram_piletrain.csv",
                       show_col_types = FALSE) |>
    rename(freq = freq_total) |>
    filter(freq > 0) |>
    select(word1, word2, freq) |>
    mutate(corpus = "Pile (~300B tok, 1 ep)")

  bind_rows(babylm_raw, pile_raw) |>
    group_by(corpus) |>
    mutate(prob = freq / sum(freq),
           rank = rank(-freq, ties.method = "first")) |>
    ungroup()
})

corpus_colors <- c("BabyLM (150M tok, 20 ep)" = "#154733",
                   "Pile (~300B tok, 1 ep)"    = "#F0B323")

p_hist <- corpus_freq_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = log10(freq), fill = corpus, color = corpus)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(count)),
                 binwidth = 0.25, position = "identity", alpha = 0.55) +
  scale_fill_manual(values  = corpus_colors, name = NULL) +
  scale_color_manual(values = corpus_colors, name = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  labs(x = expression(log[10]~"(count)"), y = "Number of pairs") +
  theme_paper() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

p_rank <- corpus_freq_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = rank, y = prob, color = corpus)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7, alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = label_comma()) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = label_scientific()) +
  scale_color_manual(values = corpus_colors, name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Rank (log scale)", y = "Probability (log scale)") +
  theme_paper() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

p_hist + p_rank + plot_layout(ncol = 2, widths = c(1, 1))
```

The BabyLM training corpus is a 150M-token collection of child-directed and informal text (CHILDES, BNC Spoken, children's books, OpenSubtitles, Wikipedia), trained for 20 epochs. The Pile is a \~300B-token web-scraped corpus used to train the Pythia family. For each of the \~47K corpus binomials, we extracted 3-gram counts (i.e., the frequency of "word$_1$ and word$_2$" and its reverse) from each corpus via infini-gram [@liu2024infinigram]. As @fig-corpus-freq shows, the BabyLM corpus produces a highly degenerate frequency distribution: 70.7% of binomials appear exactly once, 87.4% appear at most twice, and 98.2% appear at most ten times, with a maximum of 1,095 occurrences. The Pile distribution is far richer: the median binomial appears 365 times, the 25th percentile is 62 occurrences, and the 99th percentile exceeds 77,000.

In absolute training exposure terms (accounting for BabyLM's 20 epochs), the most frequent BabyLM binomials are seen at most \~21,900 times total across all training steps, while the equivalent Pile binomials are seen over 1.5 million times in a single pass. Even the median Pile binomial (365 occurrences per pass) substantially exceeds BabyLM's total exposure for a typical singleton binomial (1 × 20 = 20 exposures). This gap in absolute exposure is why the two corpora cannot be placed on a common developmental axis, and why the frequency range available for the moderation analysis differs so sharply between them.

# Experiment 1: Supplementary Results {#sec-appendix-exp1}

This appendix provides supplementary materials for Experiment 1 (§\ref{sec-exp1}), which examined final-layer probe performance for the three BabyLM models. Subsections report full R² tables with their label-shuffle controls, and a word-level replication. Coefficients for the frequency-dependent preference regression are reported together for all models in Appendix \ref{sec-appendix-relfreq}.

## Probe and Control R² {#sec-appendix-full-r2-babylm}

Probe R² at the final hidden layer for the BabyLM models, at the binomial level by attention condition, alongside the control probe fit to randomly permuted labels on the same folds. Selectivity is the difference between the two. Control values near zero indicate that the probe recovers linguistic structure and not label artifacts or probe capacity. Each control is reported beside the R² it corresponds to.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-r2-babylm
#| tbl-cap: "Probe R² at the final hidden layer for BabyLM models, at the binomial level by attention condition, with the label-shuffle control and selectivity (R² minus control). B = binomial-held-out split; W = word-held-out split. SD across 10 folds in parentheses. Control values carry an extra decimal place because they sit near zero."
#| eval: !expr nrow(all_r2) > 0

all_r2 |>
  filter(family == "BabyLM", mode == "mean_pooled") |>
  select(model, condition, split, mean_r2, sd_r2, is_control) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from  = is_control,
              values_from = c(mean_r2, sd_r2),
              names_sep   = "_") |>
  rename(r2_main = mean_r2_FALSE, sd_main = sd_r2_FALSE,
         r2_ctrl = mean_r2_TRUE,  sd_ctrl = sd_r2_TRUE) |>
  mutate(
    condition = recode_condition(condition),
    model     = factor(model, levels = model_order),
    Split     = if_else(split == "pair_novel", "B", "W"),
    `R²`           = sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)", r2_main, sd_main),
    `Control R²`   = sprintf("%.4f (%.4f)", r2_ctrl, sd_ctrl),
    Selectivity    = sprintf("%.3f", r2_main - r2_ctrl)
  ) |>
  arrange(model, condition, split) |>
  select(Model = model, Condition = condition, Split, `R²`, `Control R²`, Selectivity) |>
  kbl(longtable = TRUE, booktabs = TRUE, linesep = "") |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 8, latex_options = c("repeat_header")) |>
  collapse_rows(columns = 1:2, latex_hline = "major") |>
  allow_group_breaks()
```

## Cross-Model Agreement on Novel Binomials {#sec-appendix-agreement}

A binomial absent from the training corpus cannot have a retrieved preference, but the model still assigns one, and that value is some deterministic function of the two words' representations. Such a function could reflect systematic knowledge, or it could be an arbitrary consequence of a particular set of weights. Probe generalization cannot distinguish these, because both are systematic functions of the input and both transfer to held-out words. Agreement between independently trained models can: an arbitrary function of one model's weights has no reason to match another's.

We therefore correlate $y_{\text{true}}$ across models on identical binomials, separately for the attested and novel sets and for both attention conditions. As a baseline we shuffle one model's values, which removes any pairing between models while preserving both distributions.

The three BabyLM models are the decisive comparison. They share a training corpus and its ordering but differ in capacity, and they are the only models for which the novel binomials are genuinely absent from training (@sec-exp2, Methods). On novel binomials they agree at $r = 0.45$ under full context and $r = 0.41$ under attention-zeroing, against a shuffled baseline of $r \approx 0.00$. In other words, preferences for binomials the models never encountered are reproducible across models of different sizes trained on the same data. They are therefore not arbitrary.

Because a Pearson correlation can in principle be carried by a minority of high-magnitude items, we checked whether the agreement is concentrated in strong preferences while the bulk of binomials agree at chance. It is not. Preferences on novel binomials are not weak to begin with: median $|y_{\text{true}}|$ ranges from 1.79 to 3.21 across the three models, so the preferred ordering is between roughly six and twenty-five times more likely, and only 9% to 17% of binomials fall below 0.5. 

Rank correlations track the Pearson values closely (0.371–0.406 for BabyLM on novel binomials), and the models order the same binomial the same way on 60% to 70% of items against a chance rate of 50%, a statistic that ignores magnitude and weights every binomial equally. Stratifying by preference strength, using the third model's $|y_{\text{true}}|$ so that the bins are independent of the two series being correlated, agreement is graded but present throughout: in the weakest quintile $r = 0.30$ under full context and $0.28$ under attention-zeroing, with directional agreement near 59% in both, rising to $r = 0.61$ and 73% in the strongest. That gradient is itself informative, since agreement increasing with preference strength is the signature of a signal measured with noise rather than of an arbitrary function of a particular set of weights.

Two further patterns appear in @tbl-agreement. Agreement within a family is roughly constant across all four cells, near $r = 0.68$, whereas agreement between families falls from 0.56 on attested binomials under full context to 0.28 on novel binomials under attention-zeroing. What the models share thus survives novelty when the training corpus is shared and degrades when it is not, as expected if the preference is driven by distributional structure in the training data. This also rules out the shared sentence frame as the source of the agreement: the frame is identical for all sixteen models, so it cannot produce a gap between within-family and between-family agreement.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-agreement
#| tbl-cap: "Cross-model agreement (Pearson $r$ on $y_{\text{true}}$) for identical binomials, by item set and attention condition. Shuffled = one model's values permuted. Within-family averages over model pairs from the same family; BabyLM is broken out because its novel binomials are genuinely unseen."

read_csv(file.path(RES, "cross_model_agreement_summary.csv"),
         show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(scope %in% c("all pairs of models", "within family",
                      "between family", "within BabyLM")) |>
  mutate(
    Set       = if_else(item_set == "novel", "Novel", "Attested"),
    Condition = recode(condition, !!!condition_labels),
    Scope     = recode(scope,
                       "all pairs of models" = "All",
                       "within family"       = "Within family",
                       "between family"      = "Between family",
                       "within BabyLM"       = "Within BabyLM"),
    Scope     = factor(Scope, levels = c("All", "Within family",
                                         "Between family", "Within BabyLM")),
    Set       = factor(Set, levels = c("Attested", "Novel")),
    `$r$`     = sprintf("%.3f", mean_r),
    Shuffled  = sprintf("%.3f", shuffled_null_r)
  ) |>
  arrange(Set, Condition, Scope) |>
  select(Set, Condition, Scope, `$r$`, Shuffled) |>
  kbl(longtable = TRUE, booktabs = TRUE, linesep = "", escape = FALSE) |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 8, latex_options = c("repeat_header")) |>
  collapse_rows(columns = 1:2, latex_hline = "major") |>
  allow_group_breaks()
```

## Word-Level Replication {#sec-appendix-words-only-exp1}

We trained the MLP probe using word-level representations for the three BabyLM models to verify that the preference signal is not an artifact of mean pooling across the full binomial phrase. Under this condition the probe receives a concatenation of two word vectors extracted from isolated sentence contexts ("*the bread*", "*the butter*"), so it cannot rely on any co-occurrence signal from the two words' shared sentence context.

Binomial-held-out R² ranges from 0.31 to 0.33, within a few percentage points of the corresponding binomial-level values (0.29–0.34). The generalization pattern is preserved: word-held-out R² is consistently lower than binomial-held-out R² for all three models (word-held-out 0.18–0.20; binomial-minus-word gap 0.127–0.129), confirming that the lexical generalization cost seen at the binomial level is a property of the preference encoding itself rather than an artifact of the mean-pooled representation. The frequency-dependent preference regression was fit at the binomial level only, so it has no word-level counterpart. Full results are in @tbl-r2-babylm-words-only.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-r2-babylm-words-only
#| tbl-cap: "Word-level probe R² and selectivity (main $-$ control R²) for BabyLM models (final layer). B = binomial-held-out split; W = word-held-out split. SD across 10 folds in parentheses."

all_r2 |>
  filter(family == "BabyLM", mode == "words_only", condition == "default") |>
  select(model, condition, mode, split, mean_r2, sd_r2, is_control) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from  = is_control,
              values_from = c(mean_r2, sd_r2),
              names_sep   = "_") |>
  rename(r2_main = mean_r2_FALSE, sd_main = sd_r2_FALSE,
         r2_ctrl = mean_r2_TRUE,  sd_ctrl = sd_r2_TRUE) |>
  mutate(
    selectivity = r2_main - r2_ctrl,
    mode        = recode(mode, !!!mode_labels),
    model       = factor(model, levels = model_order),
    Split       = if_else(split == "pair_novel", "B", "W"),
    `R²`        = sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)", r2_main, sd_main),
    Ctrl        = sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)", r2_ctrl,  sd_ctrl),
    Sel.        = sprintf("%.3f", selectivity)
  ) |>
  arrange(model, split) |>
  select(Model = model, Mode = mode, Split, `R²`, Ctrl, Sel.) |>
  kbl(longtable = TRUE, booktabs = TRUE, linesep = "") |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 8, latex_options = c("repeat_header")) |>
  collapse_rows(columns = 1:2, latex_hline = "major") |>
  allow_group_breaks()
```

# Experiment 2: Supplementary Results {#sec-appendix-exp2}

This appendix provides supplementary materials for Experiment 2 (§\ref{sec-exp2}), which examined final-layer representations across all 16 models from five families. Subsections report full R² tables with their label-shuffle controls, and a word-level replication. Coefficients for the frequency-dependent preference regression are in Appendix \ref{sec-appendix-relfreq}.

## Probe and Control R² {#sec-appendix-full-r2}

Probe R² for all 16 models at the final hidden layer, binomial-level input mode, by attention condition and cross-validation split, alongside the label-shuffle control fit on the same folds and the resulting selectivity. B = binomial-held-out; W = word-held-out. SD across 10 folds in parentheses.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-r2
#| tbl-cap: "Probe R² at the final hidden layer for all 16 models, at the binomial level by attention condition, with the label-shuffle control and selectivity (R² minus control). B = binomial-held-out split; W = word-held-out split. SD across 10 folds in parentheses. Control values carry an extra decimal place because they sit near zero."
#| eval: !expr nrow(all_r2) > 0

all_r2 |>
  filter(mode == "mean_pooled") |>
  select(model, family, condition, mode, split, mean_r2, sd_r2, is_control) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from  = is_control,
              values_from = c(mean_r2, sd_r2),
              names_sep   = "_") |>
  rename(r2_main = mean_r2_FALSE, sd_main = sd_r2_FALSE,
         r2_ctrl = mean_r2_TRUE,  sd_ctrl = sd_r2_TRUE) |>
  mutate(
    condition = recode_condition(condition),
    model     = factor(model, levels = model_order),
    Split     = if_else(split == "pair_novel", "B", "W"),
    `R²`         = sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)", r2_main, sd_main),
    `Control R²` = sprintf("%.4f (%.4f)", r2_ctrl, sd_ctrl),
    Selectivity  = sprintf("%.3f", r2_main - r2_ctrl)
  ) |>
  arrange(model, condition, split) |>
  select(Model = model, Condition = condition, Split, `R²`, `Control R²`, Selectivity) |>
  kbl(longtable = TRUE, booktabs = TRUE, linesep = "") |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 7, latex_options = c("scale_down", "repeat_header")) |>
  collapse_rows(columns = 1:2, latex_hline = "major") |>
  allow_group_breaks()
```

## Word-Level Replication {#sec-appendix-words-only-exp2}

Across all 16 models, word-level probing reproduces the main findings from Experiment 2. Binomial-held-out R² is slightly lower than the corresponding binomial-level values (by roughly 5–10 percentage points for most large-scale models), but rank order across families and the generalization pattern (binomial-held-out \> word-held-out) are preserved in every case. For GPT-2, binomial-held-out R² under word-level probing ranges from 0.46 to 0.62 (vs. 0.49–0.65 at the binomial level); for Pythia, 0.51–0.57 (vs. 0.53–0.59); for OLMo, 0.52–0.57 (vs. 0.56–0.62); for Llama, 0.36–0.45 (vs. 0.43–0.55). The generalization gaps (binomial-held-out minus word-held-out) range from 0.044 to 0.073 across large-scale models, closely matching the corresponding binomial-level gaps (0.035–0.080). Full results are in @tbl-r2-words-only.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-r2-words-only
#| tbl-cap: "Word-level probe R² and selectivity (main $-$ control R²) for all 16 models (final layer). B = binomial-held-out split; W = word-held-out split. SD across 10 folds in parentheses."

all_r2 |>
  filter(mode == "words_only", condition == "default") |>
  select(family, model, condition, mode, split, mean_r2, sd_r2, is_control) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from  = is_control,
              values_from = c(mean_r2, sd_r2),
              names_sep   = "_") |>
  rename(r2_main = mean_r2_FALSE, sd_main = sd_r2_FALSE,
         r2_ctrl = mean_r2_TRUE,  sd_ctrl = sd_r2_TRUE) |>
  mutate(
    selectivity = r2_main - r2_ctrl,
    mode        = recode(mode, !!!mode_labels),
    model       = factor(model, levels = model_order),
    Split       = if_else(split == "pair_novel", "B", "W"),
    `R²`        = sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)", r2_main, sd_main),
    Ctrl        = sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)", r2_ctrl,  sd_ctrl),
    Sel.        = sprintf("%.3f", selectivity)
  ) |>
  arrange(family, model, split) |>
  select(Family = family, Model = model, Mode = mode, Split, `R²`, Ctrl, Sel.) |>
  kbl(longtable = TRUE, booktabs = TRUE, linesep = "") |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 8, latex_options = c("repeat_header")) |>
  collapse_rows(columns = 1:3, latex_hline = "major") |>
  allow_group_breaks()
```

# Experiment 3: Supplementary Results {#sec-appendix-exp3}

This appendix provides supplementary materials for Experiment 3 (§\ref{sec-exp3}), which tracked probe R² and the frequency-dependent preference regression across training checkpoints for BabyLM and Pythia. Subsections report full numerical checkpoint tables and a word-level replication of the probe results.

## Checkpoint Probe Tables {#sec-appendix-ckpt-tables}

Full numerical results for the Experiment 3 checkpoint analysis. Tables report probe R² (binomial-held-out and word-held-out) and the coefficients of @eq-relfreq for BabyLM and Pythia across training checkpoints, for the binomial-level (mean-pooled) representation under full-context and attention-zeroed conditions.

```{r}
#| echo: false

make_ckpt_r2_tbl <- function(df, cond_val, mode_val) {
  df |>
    filter(condition == cond_val, mode == mode_val,
           split %in% c("pair_novel", "word_novel")) |>
    select(model, step, tokens_M, split, mean_r2, sd_r2, is_control) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = is_control, values_from = c(mean_r2, sd_r2),
                names_sep = "_") |>
    rename(r2_main = mean_r2_FALSE, sd_main = sd_r2_FALSE,
           r2_ctrl = mean_r2_TRUE,  sd_ctrl = sd_r2_TRUE) |>
    mutate(
      model  = factor(model, levels = model_order),
      Split  = if_else(split == "pair_novel", "B", "W"),
      Tokens = sprintf("%.0f M", tokens_M),
      `R²`   = sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)", r2_main, sd_main),
      Ctrl   = sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)", r2_ctrl,  sd_ctrl),
      Sel.   = sprintf("%.3f", r2_main - r2_ctrl)
    ) |>
    arrange(model, step, split) |>
    select(Model = model, Step = step, Tokens, Split, `R²`, Ctrl, Sel.) |>
    kbl(longtable = TRUE, booktabs = TRUE, linesep = "") |>
    kable_styling(font_size = 8, latex_options = c("repeat_header")) |>
    collapse_rows(columns = 1:2, latex_hline = "major") |>
  allow_group_breaks()
}

```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-r2-checkpoints-babylm-default-mean
#| tbl-cap: "BabyLM checkpoint probe R²:full context, binomial-level. B = binomial-held-out; W = word-held-out. SD in parentheses."

if (nrow(babylm_ckpt_r2) > 0)
  make_ckpt_r2_tbl(babylm_ckpt_r2, "default", "mean_pooled")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-r2-checkpoints-babylm-attn-mean
#| tbl-cap: "BabyLM checkpoint probe R²:attention-zeroed, binomial-level."

if (nrow(babylm_ckpt_r2) > 0)
  make_ckpt_r2_tbl(babylm_ckpt_r2, "attn_zeroed", "mean_pooled")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-r2-checkpoints-pythia-default-mean
#| tbl-cap: "Pythia checkpoint probe R²:full context, binomial-level."

if (nrow(pythia_ckpt_r2) > 0)
  make_ckpt_r2_tbl(pythia_ckpt_r2, "default", "mean_pooled")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-r2-checkpoints-pythia-attn-mean
#| tbl-cap: "Pythia checkpoint probe R²:attention-zeroed, binomial-level."

if (nrow(pythia_ckpt_r2) > 0)
  make_ckpt_r2_tbl(pythia_ckpt_r2, "attn_zeroed", "mean_pooled")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-relfreq-checkpoints
#| tbl-cap: "Frequency-dependent preference regression (@eq-relfreq) at every training checkpoint, both attention conditions. `y_true` and `y_pred` are z-scored within each fit; `rel_freq` is a proportion from $-0.5$ to $+0.5$ and `log_freq` is centered but not scaled, so both mean the same thing in every corpus. 95\\% credible intervals in brackets."
#| eval: !expr nrow(relfreq_ckpt) > 0

tt2 <- function(x) paste0("\\texttt{", gsub("_", "\\\\_", x), "}")

relfreq_ckpt |>
  arrange(model, condition != "default", step) |>
  mutate(Condition = recode_condition(condition),
         a = sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]", pred_mean, pred_lo, pred_hi),
         b = sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]", rel_mean,  rel_lo,  rel_hi),
         c = sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]", pred_x_mean, pred_x_lo, pred_x_hi),
         d = sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]", rel_x_mean,  rel_x_lo,  rel_x_hi)) |>
  select(Model = model, Step = step, Condition, a, b, c, d) |>
  kbl(longtable = TRUE, booktabs = TRUE, linesep = "", escape = FALSE,
      col.names = c("Model", "Step", "Condition", tt2("y_pred"), tt2("rel_freq"),
                    paste(tt2("y_pred"), "$\\times$", tt2("log_freq")),
                    paste(tt2("rel_freq"), "$\\times$", tt2("log_freq")))) |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 6, latex_options = c("scale_down", "repeat_header")) |>
  collapse_rows(columns = 1, latex_hline = "major") |>
  allow_group_breaks()
```

## Word-Level Replication {#sec-appendix-words-only-exp3}

Word-level probe results across BabyLM and Pythia checkpoints replicate the key patterns from the binomial-level analysis. The generalization gap (binomial-held-out minus word-held-out) is largest at the earliest checkpoints and shrinks over the course of training. For BabyLM, the gap at the first checkpoint ranges from 0.15 to 0.36 across model sizes, narrowing to 0.13–0.14 by the final checkpoint, the same qualitative trajectory observed at the binomial level. Full R² results are in @tbl-r2-checkpoints-babylm-default-words and @tbl-r2-checkpoints-pythia-default-words. The frequency-dependent preference regression was fit at the binomial level only, so it has no word-level counterpart here; its checkpoint coefficients are in @tbl-relfreq-checkpoints.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-r2-checkpoints-babylm-default-words
#| tbl-cap: "BabyLM checkpoint probe R²:full context, word-level. B = binomial-held-out; W = word-held-out. SD in parentheses."

if (nrow(babylm_ckpt_r2) > 0)
  make_ckpt_r2_tbl(babylm_ckpt_r2, "default", "words_only")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-r2-checkpoints-pythia-default-words
#| tbl-cap: "Pythia checkpoint probe R²:full context, word-level. B = binomial-held-out; W = word-held-out. SD in parentheses."

if (nrow(pythia_ckpt_r2) > 0)
  make_ckpt_r2_tbl(pythia_ckpt_r2, "default", "words_only")
```
